113.title: The flower
113.hook: why it's fresh; impermanence on a plate
113.howItsDone: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning, taking down the previous day's, and often choose flowers or leaves associated with a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, lotus for Lakshmi, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deepa, the lamp. Your line was one flame. Did you let one small light be the first one last night? Day one hundred and thirteen.

Early morning, outside a Hindu temple, in India or in New Jersey. Near the gate, someone is selling flowers. Marigolds strung into long orange ropes. Jasmine in little bundles. A pile of red hibiscus. They'll all be gone by noon, and by tomorrow they'll be wilted. So why does anyone buy them? Why not a silk flower that lasts a year, dusted once a month? That's the question hiding on the third object of the shelf. Today: the flower.
screen: `FLOWER SELLERS AT THE GATE.` → `GONE BY TOMORROW.` → `WHY NOT A SILK ONE?`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is pushpa, flower. It's a standard offering in puja, and it comes with a small set of habits that tell you what it's for. Flowers are often picked or bought fresh for the morning. Yesterday's flowers are taken down and replaced. A flower that fell on the ground is usually not offered. And a flower meant for the shrine is often left unsmelled: the first enjoyment of it isn't the giver's. Different forms of the divine have their favorites. Red hibiscus often goes to Ganesha and to the Goddess. The lotus goes with Lakshmi. For Shiva, people offer the three-part leaf of the bilva tree. For Vishnu and Krishna, a leaf of tulsi, holy basil. And the offering doesn't have to be grand. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that when someone offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. Four ordinary things. The heart doing the offering is what's weighed. Now the part the flower teaches by itself. You set it down in the morning, and by evening it's drooping. You're offering something that won't last. That's not a flaw. It's honest. Everything on the plate, including the person holding the plate, is on its way somewhere. So you don't offer it once and keep it forever. You do it again tomorrow. Fresh, daily.
screen: `PUSHPA — THE FLOWER.` · `FRESH, NOT SMELLED FIRST.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WILTED BY EVENING, SO AGAIN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: If there's a flower or a leaf near you, a houseplant, a weed outside, a blossom on the table, take one gently, or just go and look at it where it grows. If not, picture one. Look at it closely. The color. The veins. The tiny imperfect edge. It won't look like this tomorrow. Now set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, next to a photo of someone you love. If you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor. Then just sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Pushpa. The flower: offered fresh, left unsmelled, gone by evening, and brought again the next day. Today's word.
Your line: fresh, daily. Today, pick one small thing you usually do on autopilot and do it fresh, as if for the first time. Day one hundred and thirteen.

114.title: The bell
114.howItsDone: Many Hindus ring a small hand bell at the start of puja and during arti, often saying a short traditional verse, and many ring the large bell at a temple's entrance as they walk in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pushpa, the flower. Your line was fresh, daily. Did you do one ordinary thing as if it were the first time? Day one hundred and fourteen.

A teacher walks into a noisy classroom and doesn't shout. She just taps a glass with a pen. Ting. And thirty kids look up. A wedding toast works the same way. So does the chime before a flight announcement. One clean sound, and a room full of scattered attention turns and faces the same way. Hindu homes and temples have known this trick for a very long time. It's the fourth object on the shelf, the small one with the handle, the one you don't just look at. Today: the bell.
screen: `A PEN AGAINST A GLASS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM LOOKS UP.` → `TODAY: THE BELL.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is ghanta, bell. At home it's usually a small brass hand bell, and if you look at the top of the handle you'll often find a little figure: Garuda the eagle for Vishnu's devotees, Nandi the bull for Shiva's, sometimes Hanuman. In temples, bigger bells hang at the entrance, and people ring one as they walk in. Why a bell? People give a few answers, and they sit side by side. The first is an invitation. Many priests and families say a short traditional verse as they ring it, asking the gods to come and sending away whatever would get in the way. The bell announces: something is starting. The second answer is about the room. A sharp, bright ring cuts through the hum of a house, the traffic, the television in the next room. It clears the air the way the pen on the glass did. And the third answer is about you. Ring a good bell and listen. There's the strike, then a long shimmering tail that fades, and fades, and fades. Some people say that fading ring echoes Om, the sound from day two. You can't follow that sound to its end while you're thinking about your email. So by the time it's gone, you're here. That's why the bell often rings at the start of puja, and again through arti. It isn't decoration. It's how you arrive.
screen: `GHANTA — THE BELL.` · `AN INVITATION: SOMETHING STARTS.` · `A RING THAT CLEARS THE ROOM.` · `FOLLOW IT TO SILENCE: ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: If you have a bell, pick it up. If not, a glass and a spoon will do, or a singing bowl, or just imagine the sound. Sit comfortably. Strike it once, gently. Then don't move. Follow the sound as it thins out, all the way down, until you honestly can't tell whether you still hear it. When it's gone, notice where you are. The room. The chair. Your breath. You've arrived. Now let the app's bell do the same work for you. The bell holds the time.
Ghanta. The bell: rung at the start of puja and through arti, to invite, to clear the room, and to bring you all the way here. Today's word.
Your line: arrive. Today, when you walk into a room that matters, pause for one breath at the door, like the ring of a bell, before you start. Day one hundred and fourteen.

115.title: The water
115.howItsDone: In puja, many Hindus offer water to the deity as to an honored guest (for the feet, the hands and the mouth), sip a little themselves to purify before beginning, pour water toward the rising sun in the morning, and receive offered water back afterward as a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghanta, the bell. Your line was arrive. Did you pause for one breath at a door before you walked in? Day one hundred and fifteen.

A guest you love arrives after a long trip. Before the food, before the stories, someone hands them a glass of water and shows them where to wash up. In a lot of homes, that's the host's first move. Now move that same welcome to a small shelf in the corner of a kitchen, and offer it every morning. The last of the five objects is the plainest one. It's usually a small copper or brass cup and a tiny spoon. Today: the water.
screen: `A GUEST ARRIVES.` → `FIRST, A GLASS OF WATER.` → `TODAY: THE WATER.`

segments.voice: In puja, the divine is welcomed the way you'd welcome the most honored guest you can imagine. And water does three jobs in that welcome. The first is washing. A few drops are offered for the guest's feet, a few for the hands, a few to rinse the mouth, each with its own Sanskrit name, just as you'd offer a traveler a basin. Worshippers often sip a little water themselves at the start, from the palm of the right hand, to make themselves clean before they begin. The second job is offering. Water is poured out as a gift. In the morning, some Hindus stand facing the rising sun and pour water from a small pot, watching the stream catch the light. And remember the Gita from two days ago: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. Water is on that short list. It costs almost nothing, and it's enough. The third job is drinking. After puja, water that has been offered, sometimes mixed with tulsi leaves or used to bathe the image, is given back to the family, a few drops in the palm, and sipped. Some homes also keep a little bottle of water from the Ganga, the Ganges, a drop of which can be added. So the same small cup washes, gives and returns. Nothing about it is dramatic. That's the point. The plainest thing on the shelf teaches the plainest lesson: begin clean.
screen: `WELCOMED LIKE AN HONORED GUEST.` · `WASHING: FEET, HANDS, MOUTH.` · `OFFERING: POURED TOWARD THE SUN.` · `DRINKING: IT COMES BACK TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Get a small cup of water, or just go to a sink. Wash your hands slowly, as if you were getting ready to greet someone important. Feel the water on your fingers. Then pour a few drops somewhere as a gift: a houseplant, the soil outside, or into the cup of your corner. If you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor. Then take one small sip, and notice it going down. Washed, given, received. Clean. The bell holds the time.
The water. The plainest offering: it washes the honored guest, it's poured out as a gift, and it comes back to be sipped. Today's word.
Your line: clean. Today, the next time you hand someone a glass of water, hand it the way a host would to an honored guest. Day one hundred and fifteen.

116.title: The sweet
116.howItsDone: Many Hindus place a small portion of food, often a sweet or fruit, before the image at the home shrine as naivedya, wait a few moments, and then share it as prasad with everyone in the house and any guests.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water: washed, given, received. Your line was clean. Did you hand someone a glass of water like a host? Day one hundred and sixteen.

A grandmother is in her kitchen making laddus, little round sweets, for a festival. The grandkids hover. One reaches for the tray. And she swats his hand away, not unkindly. Not yet. First they go to the shrine. The child sighs, the way children have sighed in that kitchen for generations. Ten minutes later, the same tray comes back, and now she presses one into his palm, smiling. Same sweet. Same tray. But something happened in those ten minutes, and the children in that house learn it long before they can explain it. Today: the sweet.
screen: `NOT YET.` → `FIRST, THE SHRINE.` → `THEN, INTO YOUR PALM.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is naivedya: food offered to the divine. It can be a whole meal or a spoonful of sugar crystals, a banana, a cup of milk, a laddu. Sweets are the classic. Here's roughly how it goes at home. The food is cooked with care, and the cook often doesn't even taste it while it's being made for the shrine: the first taste isn't theirs. A little is set before the image on a clean plate, sometimes with a tulsi leaf on top. Water may be sprinkled around it. It sits there for a few moments. Some families draw a curtain, or simply look away, as if giving a guest privacy to eat. Then the plate comes back. And here's the turn. Once it's been offered, the food isn't naivedya anymore. It's prasad, the word you met back on day twenty-eight: grace, the gift that returns. And prasad is for sharing. It goes to everyone in the house, to the guest at the door, to the neighbor. People receive it in the right hand, often with a small bow, and people try not to refuse it. The Bhagavad Gita has a blunt way of putting the idea: those who eat what remains after an offering are freed from wrong, but those who cook only for themselves, it says, eat their own wrongdoing. Food that's kept is just food. Food that's offered and handed round becomes something else. That's what happened in those ten minutes in the kitchen.
screen: `NAIVEDYA — FOOD OFFERED.` · `THE FIRST TASTE ISN'T YOURS.` · `IT RETURNS AS PRASAD.` · `COOK ONLY FOR YOURSELF, AND…`

segments.voice: Find something small to eat: a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a few raisins. Before you eat it, set it down in front of you, or in your corner, and pause. If you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor. If not, just hold it as a gift you didn't make entirely yourself: the sun, the farmer, the truck driver. Wait a few breaths. Then, if you can, break it in two, and put half aside for someone else. Eat your half slowly. The bell holds the time.
Naivedya. Food offered to the divine before anyone eats, which comes back as prasad to be shared. Today's word.
Your line: shared. Today, give away the first piece of something you were about to enjoy alone: the first slice, the first cup, the first bite. Day one hundred and sixteen.

117.title: Morning puja
117.hook: the whole thing in four minutes
117.howItsDone: Many Hindu households do a short daily puja at the home shrine in the morning: ringing a bell, lighting a lamp, offering flowers, water and food, saying a mantra or a deity's name, bowing, and sharing the offered food as prasad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naivedya, the sweet that goes to the shrine first. Your line was shared. Did you give away a first piece of something? Day one hundred and seventeen.

This week began with five objects and a corner that's yours. Then one flame, the lamp. A flower, fresh, daily. A bell that helps you arrive. Water: washed, given, received. And a sweet that goes to the shrine first and comes back to be shared. Six days, six pieces, laid out on the table like parts of a watch. Today we put the watch together. People sometimes imagine puja as a long, complicated ceremony that only a priest can run. At a temple on a festival day, it can be. At home, on a Tuesday, before work, it can be four minutes.
screen: `A WEEK OF PIECES.` → `NOT JUST FOR PRIESTS.` → `TODAY: PUT IT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Puja, the word from day eight, means honoring, worship, and the old line from that day still holds: attention is an offering. Full temple worship can have sixteen services, the whole welcome of a royal guest. Many homes use a short form, and old manuals even name a five-part version: fragrance, flower, incense, lamp and food. Your week covered three of those five, the flower, the lamp and the food, and added a bell and water. So here's one simple morning shape. Families do it in different orders, and none is the only right one. First, begin clean: wash, or sip a little water. Then ring the bell, and let it bring you here. Light the lamp. Offer a flower, and a few drops of water. Set down something sweet. Then comes the heart of it: a few moments of mantra: Om, or the one from the mantra days that fits you, Om namah shivaya or the Gayatri, or simply the name you honor, said quietly. Then pranam, the bow from day four: hands together, head down. And last, take a little of the sweet back as prasad, and share the rest later. That's it. Bell, lamp, flower, water, food, name, bow. Some mornings you'll do all of it. Some mornings you'll just light the lamp and bow. Even that small version is attention given, the line from day eight. The point was never the full list. The point is that before the day grabs you, something else gets the first four minutes.
screen: `PUJA — ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.` · `A FIVE-PART FORM FOR HOME.` · `BELL, LAMP, FLOWER, WATER, FOOD.` · `A NAME, A BOW, THE SWEET RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Let's do it together, however small your corner is, even if it's only in your mind. Ring the bell, or tap a glass, and listen until it fades. Light the lamp, or picture it. Set down a flower or a leaf. A few drops of water. A small piece of something sweet. Now, quietly, say your mantra or a name you honor, if you'd like, a few times. Hands together. Bow. The rest of the time is yours to sit in front of it. The bell holds the time.
Morning puja. The home shrine, put together: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow, before the day begins. Today's word.

Your line: four minutes. Tomorrow morning, before your phone, give four minutes to your corner, any version of it. That's the week. Tomorrow we move to the other end of the day. Day one hundred and seventeen.

118.title: The hour
118.hook: the three junctions of the day
118.howItsDone: Traditionally, sandhyavandana, a prayer centered on the Gayatri mantra, is said at dawn, noon and dusk, especially by those who wear the sacred thread; in many Hindu homes, a lamp is lit at dusk and the household pauses as it's lit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning puja: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow. Your line was four minutes. Did the corner get the first four minutes of your day? Day one hundred and eighteen.

There's a moment on a summer evening when the streetlights haven't come on yet, but the sky has stopped being day. The colors go strange. The birds get loud, then quiet. Someone on a porch says, look at that, and nobody answers, because everyone's looking. Photographers call it the golden hour, and the blue hour after it. A new week starts today, the week of sunset and arti, and it opens with a question: when? Today: the hour.
screen: `NOT DAY, NOT YET NIGHT.` → `A NEW WEEK: SUNSET AND ARTI.` → `TODAY: THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is sandhya. It comes from a word for joining, a junction, the place where two things meet. So sandhya means twilight, and more than that: the joints of the day. Tradition names three. Dawn, where night meets day. Noon, where the morning turns into afternoon. And dusk, where day meets night. These are the hours set aside for prayer. There's a whole ancient practice named for them, sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, and at its heart is the Gayatri, the mantra you met on day one hundred and eight, a prayer to the light of the sun. Traditionally it's kept by those who wear the sacred thread, and other Hindus keep a simpler version of the idea. Why the junctions? Here are a few ways people explain it. A junction belongs to neither side, so it's a natural doorway, a gap in the ordinary. The light is changing, and when the light changes, people notice. And practically, dawn and dusk are when a busy household stops anyway: before the day's work, after it. So at home, dusk often has its own small rite. Someone lights the lamp as the sun goes down, the evening lamp, and in some families people stop what they're doing when it's lit, even for a moment. The day is being handed over to the night, and someone should be there for it.
screen: `SANDHYA — A JOINING, A JUNCTION.` · `DAWN, NOON, DUSK.` · `SANDHYAVANDANA AND THE GAYATRI.` · `THE EVENING LAMP AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: If it's near dawn or dusk where you are, find a window, or step outside. If it isn't, remember the last sunset you really watched. Sit, and look at the light, not at anything in particular. Notice that it's changing even as you watch. Nothing is being asked of you but to be present at the joining. If you pray, this is one of the hours tradition sets aside. If not, simply be the one who noticed the day turning. The bell holds the time.
Sandhya. A joining: the twilight, and the three junctions of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, set aside for prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the junction. Today, catch one of the three, dawn, noon or dusk, and give it one full minute of your attention. Day one hundred and eighteen.

119.title: Arti at home
119.howItsDone: At home, many Hindus perform arti at dawn and at dusk by circling a small ghee lamp or burning camphor clockwise before the image, often in a pattern from the feet to the face, while a bell is rung and an arti song is sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhya, the hour where two things join. Your line was the junction. Which one did you catch: dawn, noon or dusk? Day one hundred and nineteen.

If you've ever seen videos of the evening arti on the banks of the Ganga, you know the picture. Priests in a row, each holding up a huge brass lamp with a crown of flames, swinging it in slow circles as bells clang and thousands of people sing. The river turns gold. It's one of the most famous sights in India. Now shrink it. A kitchen. A shelf. One small plate with one small flame, held by someone in socks, and maybe a kid ringing a bell a little too hard. Same act. Today: arti at home.
screen: `THE GANGA AT DUSK, LAMPS BLAZING.` → `NOW SHRINK IT.` → `ONE PLATE, ONE FLAME, AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Arti was your fourteenth word, way back in camp one: light passed hand to hand. That was what it means. Today is how it's done. The word comes from the Sanskrit aratrika, often explained as a rite done at night, or one that removes darkness. At home, the lamp is usually a small plate with a ghee wick, or a piece of camphor that burns bright and fast. You stand in front of the image, and you move the flame in slow circles, clockwise. Many people make a pattern: a few circles in front of the feet, a few at the middle, a few at the face, then around the whole form. Families do it in different ways, and there's no single count everyone agrees on. While the flame circles, someone rings the bell with the other hand, or someone else rings it for you. And there's singing: an arti song, which you'll learn tomorrow. Why circle? People give a few answers. Circling is what you do around something at the center of your life: a flame circled in front of the image puts the divine at the center. It also lets the light fall on every part of the form, as if you were seeing it, all of it, by lamplight. And people often point out that camphor burns without leaving any ash behind. Some say that's the whole hope of devotion: to burn bright, give light, and leave no ego behind.
screen: `ARTI — FROM ARATRIKA.` · `A SMALL FLAME, CIRCLED CLOCKWISE.` · `FEET, MIDDLE, FACE, THE WHOLE.` · `CAMPHOR LEAVES NO ASH.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it, and hold it on a plate or holder steady in your right hand. If not, use your open hand, or just your eyes. In front of an image, a photo, or simply a window, make a few slow circles, clockwise. A few low, a few in the middle, a few at the height of a face. Go slowly enough that you can watch the light move. Then set it down, and sit with the flame. The bell holds the time.
Camphor, the flame that burns bright and leaves no ash: circled clockwise at home in front of the image, with a bell and a song, so the light falls on every part. Today's word.
Your line: light, circled. Today, notice one thing you keep circling back to, and ask whether it deserves the center. Day one hundred and nineteen.

match.prompt: how it's done — tap the pairs.
pairs: burns bright and leaves no ash

myth: arti needs a priest and a riverbank
at home it's one small flame on a plate, often done by the family itself.
everyone agrees on the exact number of circles
families do it in different ways; there's no single count.
camphor is used partly because it leaves no ash
some say that's the hope of devotion: burn bright and leave no ego behind.

fork.setup: you're holding the arti flame in front of the image for the first time. which way do you circle it?
fork.reveal: clockwise. circling keeps the divine at the center, and many families move from the feet to the face to the whole form.

original.note: Hindi ārtī, from Sanskrit ārātrika: the rite of the circled lamp.

trapdoor: what you thought: waving a candle around.
what it means: a flame circled clockwise before the image, with a bell and a song, so the light falls on every part of the form.
what a scholar hears: arti derives from ārātrika, variously explained as a nighttime rite or as the removal of darkness; camphor's residue-free burning is a common image for the dissolving of ego.
